title: The Cosmic Treasure Chest
caption: The southern Virgo Cluster, imaged by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
celestial: Virgo Cluster · constellation Virgo · about 55 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Countless specks of light fill this wide field, among them bright stars ranging from blue to red, nearby blue spiral galaxies and distant red groups of galaxies. The scene is the southern part of the Virgo Cluster, about 55 million light-years from Earth and the closest large gathering of galaxies to the Milky Way. It was one of the first images released by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Apart from a handful of foreground stars in our own galaxy, nearly every dot here is a galaxy, around 10 million of them. Even so, that is only about 0.05% of the roughly 20 billion that Rubin expects to record over the 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).

The picture is a sample of how that survey will work. It combines 1185 exposures gathered over just 7 nights through different color filters, and stacking them brings out faint detail no single exposure could capture. Rubin will return to this patch of sky many times, watching for supernovae and other brief events.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (326.38 x 171.74 arcminutes) and distance (55 million light years), the frame spans roughly 5.2 million × 2.7 million light-years. Its light set out about 55 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken with the LSST Camera on Rubin Observatory's Simonyi Survey Telescope in optical light through u, g, r and i filters. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
filters: 372 nm · Optical u (Simonyi Survey Telescope LSSTCam)
480 nm · Optical g (Simonyi Survey Telescope LSSTCam)
622 nm · Optical r (Simonyi Survey Telescope LSSTCam)
755 nm · Optical i (Simonyi Survey Telescope LSSTCam)
understand.eye: The picture stacks many exposures, gathering far more light than the eye can and revealing galaxies much too faint to see directly.

explore: Asteroids moving through our Solar System appear as multicolored streaks, because each one sat in a different place in every exposure. A single Rubin exposure covers 10 square degrees, about 45 full Moons, while this combined image spans 15 square degrees.

The 3200-megapixel LSST Camera that took it is described as the largest digital camera in the world. By mapping how galaxies like these are shaped and spread out, scientists hope to probe dark matter and dark energy.
alt: A wide field scattered with stars ranging from blue to red and many small galaxies, including blue spirals and red galaxy groups.
